description: Christine McVie's shimmering love song from Tango in the Night — a half-speed-guitar intro, a Highwayman video, and a pop gem that keeps returning to the charts via ads and covers.

pops.text: That twinkling intro is a trick of the tape: co-producer Richard Dashut called it 'a half-speed acoustic guitar and electric combined.' McVie recalled Buckingham slowing the tape way down, playing the parts slowly, and at full speed it sounded 'bloody amazing.'
Christine McVie wrote this one entirely by herself and sings lead. Direct, melodic love songs were her specialty — and this may be her most buoyant.

It's from Tango in the Night, Fleetwood Mac's 14th studio album and their first in five years. It was also the final studio album to feature the classic five-piece lineup of Buckingham, Nicks, both McVies and Fleetwood.
Lindsey Buckingham produced with Richard Dashut, and his toolkit shows in the credits: guitars, keyboards, Fairlight CMI synthesizer and programming, all under McVie's vocal.
An earlier version left off harmonies Stevie Nicks had recorded — Rolling Stone reports the omission led to a heated argument before the finished mix.

The video ignores the love song completely: director Alex Proyas — later of The Crow and Dark City — dramatized Alfred Noyes' poem 'The Highwayman.' Two versions exist, one with band members superimposed and one with no band at all.
The video's story was built on six interior sets constructed over two weeks. All that work for a song where, lyrically, almost nothing happens except being in love.
Chart report: No. 14 on the Billboard Hot 100, three weeks at No. 1 on Adult Contemporary, No. 4 in the UK — and No. 1 in Belgium.
The 12-inch single carried extended dance and dub versions, and 'Everywhere' marked the band's first CD single release in most territories. Its B-side was the album track 'When I See You Again.'

It refuses to retire: a 2013 UK ad for mobile provider 3 sent it back to No. 15, a 2022 Chevrolet EV ad took it to No. 1 on Billboard's Rock Digital Song Sales, and Niall Horan and Anne-Marie covered it for BBC Children in Need in 2021 — with McVie's blessing.

title: Everywhere

description: Mike Mills' country-tinged plea to Ingrid Schorr not to leave Athens for Rockville, Maryland. Written as punk, recorded as a joke for their manager, it became an R.E.M. live staple.

pops.text: Mike Mills wrote this in 1980, in the band's earliest days. He told American Songwriter he built it at a kitchen table on Little Oconee Street in Athens, Georgia, around a turnaround inspired by part of Simon & Garfunkel's 'Mrs. Robinson.'

It's a real plea to a real person: Mills was seeing Ingrid Schorr, who was heading back to Rockville, Maryland, where her parents lived. As he wrote, a summer trip morphed into a lover leaving for good.

Mills later clarified they were seeing each other but were not, in his telling, boyfriend and girlfriend. Schorr became a journalist and wrote about the surreal experience of inspiring the song — and her amusement at fans' inaccurate versions of the story.
Peter Buck said the song was originally performed in a punk/thrash style. The slow country arrangement on the record began as a joke aimed at manager Bertis Downs, who loved the song.
It's on Reckoning, R.E.M.'s second album, recorded at Reflection Sound in Charlotte, North Carolina, with returning producers Mitch Easter and Don Dixon.
Mills did the bulk of the writing, but the credit reads Berry/Buck/Mills/Stipe. Crediting all four members equally, whoever did the work, was the band's standing habit.

Michael Stipe sings lead on the album version, with Mills and Bill Berry harmonizing. Mills noticed years later that the chorus stays in unison until the word 'Rockville,' where it breaks into three-part harmony.
That's Mills on piano, too, alongside his bass. The keys are a big part of why this Athens indie band suddenly sounds like a country band.

Released October 16, 1984 as Reckoning's second and final single, it failed to chart on either the Billboard Hot 100 or the UK Singles Chart. The single edit trimmed the 4:33 album version to 3:55, with a live 'Catapult' on the B-side.
In concert, Mills usually takes the lead vocal himself. A live version turned up as the B-side of 'Leaving New York' in 2004, and 10,000 Maniacs covered the song in 1992.

title: (Don't Go Back To) Rockville

description: A train song for the Southern Crescent from Fables of the Reconstruction, written in about five minutes. Its harmonica blows like a train whistle over Peter Buck's jangling riff.

pops.text: This one came together in about five minutes: Bill Berry had the verse, left to buy beans or rice at the market, and Peter Buck had the chorus and intro riff waiting when he got back.
Driver 8's train is the Southern Crescent, the Southern Railway passenger train that ran until 1979. It still runs today, with fewer stops, as Amtrak's Crescent.

Hear that whistle? It's a harmonica played to mimic a train whistle. Mike Mills agreed in a 2024 interview that the song is melancholic — trains are wistful, and E minor, he noted, is a great sad key.
Fables of the Reconstruction was produced by Joe Boyd and recorded at Livingston Studios in London — R.E.M.'s first album recorded outside the United States.
The album is a Southern Gothic concept record, and it reached No. 28 on the Billboard 200, the band's best US showing yet. It went gold in 1991.
R.E.M.HQ's own liner notes keep it simple: 'Train song from Fables with a train video to match.' The video shows Chessie System trains running around Clifton Forge, Virginia.
Released in September 1985 as the album's second single, it peaked at No. 22 on Billboard's Mainstream Rock Tracks chart. It was not released as a single in Europe.
The B-side was 'Crazy,' a cover of a song by Pylon — fellow Athens, Georgia scene-makers and one of R.E.M.'s formative local influences.
Recycling, R.E.M. style: Buck admitted in the liner notes to In Time that the verse chords of 2001's 'Imitation of Life' were unintentionally taken from 'Driver 8.'
Jason Isbell covered it on Georgia Blue, his 2021 album of songs by Georgia artists — and the song even has a mountain bike named after it: Santa Cruz released a Driver 8 model in 2009.

title: Driver 8

description: The opening blast of Lifes Rich Pageant: a Cole Porter pun, a newly intelligible Michael Stipe, and a call to begin again that opened R.E.M.'s Hall of Fame performances.

pops.text: First things first: this is track one of Lifes Rich Pageant, R.E.M.'s fourth album, released July 28, 1986. It was never released as a single.
The title is a pun on Cole Porter's 'Begin the Beguine.' A Broadway standard, bent one syllable out of shape, becomes a call to start over.
It was written on acoustic guitars at Michael Stipe's home. The original version ran a minute longer, had five different choruses, and lacked both a melody and a bridge.
Stipe has called it 'a song of personal, political activism.' Its cast of characters includes Plymouth militia leader Miles Standish and a name-checked 'Martin Luther Zen.'
Longtime fans noticed something new in 1986: you could understand the words. As the opening track, it heralded a new clarity in Stipe's vocals after the famous mumble of the early records.
New producer Don Gehman — John Mellencamp's producer — gave Bill Berry the biggest drum sound he'd had yet. You can hear it launch this song.
The album was recorded at Mellencamp's Belmont Mall studio in Bloomington, Indiana, in spring 1986. It was only the second record ever made there; Mellencamp's Scarecrow was the first.
The album title comes from a Peter Sellers line in the Pink Panther film A Shot in the Dark: 'It's all part of life's rich pageant.'
Lifes Rich Pageant peaked at No. 21 on the Billboard album chart and became R.E.M.'s first gold record — their bridge from college radio to the mainstream.

Live, it was an early-set energizer for decades — and when R.E.M. were inducted into both the Georgia Music Hall of Fame and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, they opened their performances with it. It also opens their 2006 I.R.S.-years compilation And I Feel Fine.

title: Begin The Begin

description: A Let It Bleed deep cut with Bill Wyman on vibraphone, Nicky Hopkins on piano and Keith Richards sliding through the riff. Never a single, it later turned up in Goodfellas.

pops.text: This is track eight of nine on Let It Bleed, released December 5, 1969 — tucked in right before the closer, 'You Can't Always Get What You Want.'
Mick Jagger and Keith Richards wrote it as a tribute to Italian pop artist Mario Schifano, whom they met on the set of his film Umano Non Umano! — 'Human, Not Human!'
It was recorded in April 1969 with producer Jimmy Miller, who doesn't stay behind the glass: he plays the tambourine on the track.

That eerie, shimmering intro instrument is a vibraphone — played by bassist Bill Wyman, who handles both vibes and bass here. His vibraphone is mixed on the left channel, together with Nicky Hopkins' piano.
Hopkins' piano tinkles set the trap, then Keith Richards springs it with the main riff — and Richards also takes the slide guitar solo.
Classic Rock History ranked this the Stones' ninth-best deep cut, praising the vibraphone chimes that give the opening its 'espionage-esque' vibe.
Jagger's narrator mocks himself before anyone else can: 'I'm a fleabit peanut monkey, all my friends are junkies — that's not really true.' The song undercuts its own confession mid-line.
It was an album track only, never a single — a fan-favorite deep cut rather than a radio hit, which is exactly how its reputation grew.
Sampling afterlife: that distinctive piano progression from the intro became the opening theme 'Playing With Fire' on the Stereo MCs' 1992 album Connected.

Martin Scorsese used it in Goodfellas in 1990, and the Stones themselves revived it on stage: they played it often on the 1994–95 Voodoo Lounge Tour, and a Licks Tour performance landed on Live Licks in 2004.

title: Monkey Man

description: The Devil himself narrates history's atrocities over a hypnotic samba groove. The Beggars Banquet opener began as a Dylan-style folk song and became the Stones' most notorious recording.

pops.text: Please allow him to introduce himself: this opens Beggars Banquet, released December 6, 1968 — the Devil gets track one and the first word.
Mick Jagger wrote most of it, under the working title 'The Devil Is My Name,' after Marianne Faithfull gave him Bulgakov's novel The Master and Margarita, whose Devil visits Moscow.
It did not start as a samba. Jagger brought it in as a Dylan-esque folk ballad, and Keith Richards suggested pushing the tempo and adding percussion until it swung.
French director Jean-Luc Godard filmed the June 1968 Olympic Studios sessions for his film One Plus One, capturing the song evolving take by take, folk sketch to samba.
That groove is a supergroup in miniature: Nicky Hopkins on piano, Rocky Dijon on congas, Bill Wyman shaking maracas — and Keith playing both the bass and the guitar solo.
The famous 'woo woo' chant was an accident. Producer Jimmy Miller kept muttering 'who, who?' in the control booth, Anita Pallenberg flagged how good it sounded, and the band adopted it.
History rewrote a lyric mid-session: the line was 'Who killed Kennedy?' until Robert F. Kennedy was assassinated on June 6, 1968, during recording — so Jagger pluralized it to 'the Kennedys.'
This performance comes from The Rolling Stones Rock and Roll Circus, filmed before a live London audience in December 1968 and directed by Michael Lindsay-Hogg.
Altamont myth-check: Meredith Hunter was not killed during this song. The Stones had stopped 'Sympathy' earlier over crowd fights; the fatal stabbing happened during 'Under My Thumb.'
Rolling Stone ranked it No. 32 on its original 500 Greatest Songs of All Time list — not bad for a track that was never released as a US or UK single in its day.

title: Sympathy For The Devil

description: A sweet-sounding country kiss-off with a needle in its pocket, from Sticky Fingers. Jagger drawls over honky-tonk guitars, promising roses on a grave — Gram Parsons' influence in full bloom.

pops.text: Official audio only — no music video was ever made. This is track nine on Sticky Fingers (1971), the Stones' first album on their own label, wrapped in Andy Warhol's working-zipper cover.
It was recorded at Olympic Studios in London, with sessions running from December 1969 into April 1970 — a full year before the album came out.
That convincing country twang has a source: Keith Richards' close friendship with Gram Parsons was pulling the Stones deep into country music at the time.
Jagger later admitted his heart was only half in the drawl. In 2003 he said the music is played completely straight, but 'I think I'm a blues singer, not a country singer.'
Listen for two honky-tonk guitars trading licks — both Keith Richards and Mick Taylor play lead lines — while founding member Ian Stewart handles the barroom piano.
Sweet tune, dark lyric: between the wedding flowers and the roses on the grave sits 'I'll be in my basement room, with a needle and a spoon' — a plain heroin reference.
The lyric bets on Kentucky Derby Day, so the Stones played it at Churchill Downs itself — the Derby's home track — during a September 2006 concert there.
It was a live regular on the 1970–72 tours, then vanished from the setlist after one 1976 outing until the band revived it on the Steel Wheels tour in 1989.
Cover magnets: by 2024, SecondHandSongs counted 61 cover versions, making it the 19th most-covered Stones song — New Riders of the Purple Sage cut it back in 1976.
Townes Van Zandt's cover plays over The Big Lebowski's closing credits. Rights holder Allen Klein first asked $150,000 — then waived the fee after hearing the Dude say 'I hate the Eagles, man!'

title: Dead Flowers

description: Official audio of the studio version from Panic's 1991 Capricorn debut. A stomping Athens tribute: the band named this jammy rocker after fellow Athens band Love Tractor, whose sound it resembled.

pops.text: Official audio only — no music video exists for this one. And no, it's not about farm equipment: 'Love Tractor' was another Athens, Georgia band, local heroes of the same scene.
John Bell has said the song began as a lick the band would jam on and crack up over, because it sounded so much like the Athens band Love Tractor. The name just stuck.
Athens newspaper The Red & Black spotted the homage in real time: reviewing the new album in August 1991, it noted the song 'Love Tractor' is dedicated to a local favorite.
An early version was cut in September 1990 at producer John Keane's Athens studio during the sessions fans know as Mom's Kitchen, alongside 'Pigeons' and 'Proving Ground.'
Those Mom's Kitchen tapes were shelved when Capricorn Records signed the band to a six-album deal in January 1991 — so they re-recorded everything properly.
Phish connection: a December 1990 demo of this song, cut at Keane's studio with Phish keyboardist Page McConnell sitting in, finally surfaced on the 2022 collection Miss Kitty's Lounge.
The album sessions road-tripped the South: Emerald Sound in Nashville, Kiva Studios in Memphis, and Duck Tape Music in Decatur, Alabama.
The keys on this record belong to T Lavitz of the Dixie Dregs, recruited to fill out Panic's sound. The self-titled album arrived July 30, 1991.
It became a set-closing weapon: at Red Rocks in June 2016, Panic segued out of Traffic's 'The Low Spark of High Heeled Boys' straight into 'Love Tractor' to end the second set.
Three decades on, it remains a cornerstone of the live show — the little Athens in-joke that turned into one of the most durable songs in the Panic catalog.

title: Love Tractor

description: John Bell turns a Farmers' Almanac tale into a rain dance: the true story of Charles Hatfield, the sewing-machine salesman who promised San Diego rain in 1916 and delivered a catastrophic flood.

pops.text: Official audio only — no music video was made. Charles Mallory Hatfield was a real man: a sewing-machine salesman who reinvented himself as a professional rainmaker.
John Bell wrote this after stumbling on Hatfield's story in a Farmers' Almanac — possibly the most Widespread Panic songwriting origin story ever.
Hatfield refused the word 'rainmaker.' He called himself a 'moisture accelerator,' and guarded a secret formula of 23 chemicals brewed in big galvanized evaporating tanks.
He worked with his brother Paul — the lyric's 'Hatfield and his brother' — building wooden towers to release the mix. Los Angeles ranchers paid him $50 in 1904, then doubled it when rain came.
The big contract: in 1915, drought-stricken San Diego voted him a $10,000 fee to fill the Morena Dam reservoir. He and Paul built a 20-foot tower beside Lake Morena.
Then came January 1916 — and the rain would not stop. Flooding around Lake Morena wrecked dams, bridges and roads across San Diego County and turned deadly.
San Diego never paid him. Paying up would have meant admitting the city had hired the flood, so the rain was officially treated as an act of God.
Hatfield took his formula to the grave in 1958 — but Hollywood got there first: his story helped inspire the play and the 1956 Burt Lancaster film The Rainmaker.
This is track two on Everyday, recorded over about five weeks starting November 1992 at Muscle Shoals Sound Studio in Alabama — the band's first album with keyboardist JoJo Hermann.
It was brand new when JoJo auditioned: just the song's fourth-ever performance came at his first acoustic set with the band in Athens on March 4, 1992. It has been a fan favorite ever since.

title: Hatfield

description: Seven-plus minutes in a roadside diner, watching the waitress move like music. A slow-burning Everyday favorite that Panic road-tested live for a full year before recording it in Muscle Shoals.

pops.text: Official audio only — no music video was ever made. 'Diner' debuted live on February 7, 1992, at The Post Office in Augusta, Georgia, more than a year before it appeared on an album.
The narrator is a down-and-out drifter nursing coffee and watching the waitress. As AllMusic's review put it, he sings of her: 'She's like natural music any way she moves.'
At 7 minutes 25 seconds, this is the longest track on Everyday — the band lets the groove simmer and stretch instead of rushing the story.
Everyday was produced by Johnny Sandlin, the Capricorn Records house producer, and recorded beginning November 5, 1992, at Muscle Shoals Sound Studio in Sheffield, Alabama.
Keyboardist John 'JoJo' Hermann had joined only months earlier — his first full show with Panic, on March 13, 1992, already included 'Diner' in the set.
Check the album cover sometime: Everyday's artwork features a then-unknown young model and actress named Angelina Jolie.
The album peaked at just No. 184 on the Billboard 200 (No. 10 on Heatseekers) — Panic's following was built in concert halls, not on the charts.
The band later shared official concert video of this one from Red Rocks: on June 24, 2017, 'Diner' opened the second set at the Colorado amphitheater.
Live, John Bell treats the middle of this song as open mic night — in Pensacola in 2019 he slipped an improvised 'Take Me to the River' rap into it.
By setlist.fm's count, Panic have played 'Diner' more than 670 times — a road-tested staple that has been on the menu for over three decades.

title: Diner

description: A Garcia-Hunter live-only favorite first released on the triple live album Europe '72, packed with whimsical name-checks from Jack the Ripper to Wolfman Jack. This cut is the Lyceum, London version from the tour's final night.

pops.text: Studio? Never happened. Archivist David Lemieux notes this song was never recorded in a studio — the Europe '72 live version is the definitive one.
It debuted on October 19, 1971 at Northrop Auditorium in Minneapolis — the very same night Keith Godchaux played his first show as a member of the Grateful Dead.

That night was a song factory: 'Tennessee Jed,' 'Jack Straw,' 'Mexicali Blues,' 'Comes a Time' and 'One More Saturday Night' also got their first performances, with 'Ramble on Rose' arriving in the second set after 'Truckin'.'
Lyricist Robert Hunter called it 'the closest to complete whimsy I've come up with,' saying he just sat down and wrote numerous verses tied around 'Did you say…'
The name-check parade starts dark: the opening verse nods to Jack the Ripper, then pivots to New York City, mojo hands and ragtime. Whimsy, indeed.

That 'Wolfman Jack' line is disc jockey Robert Weston Smith, whose border-radio show blasted across North America from Mexico. Hunter name-checked him a year before American Graffiti made him a movie face.
'Just like Crazy Otto' salutes ragtime pianist Johnny Maddox, who recorded under that name. Evangelist and ex-ballplayer Billy Sunday and Frankenstein author Mary Shelley also get shout-outs.
This recording comes from the Strand Lyceum in London on May 26, 1972 — the final night of the band's 22-show European tour.
Europe '72 was a triple live album, but not purely live: the band overdubbed lush harmony vocals back in the US, making it a live-studio hybrid.
It stayed in the repertoire right up to the summer of 1995. By the usual setlist counts, the Dead played it more than 300 times.

title: Ramble on Rose

description: A cheery murder ballad from Workingman's Dead: in fictional Fennario, a man invites a grinning wolf in for a game of cards, and the wolf collects his due. Garcia's pedal steel curls around Hunter's dream-born lyric.

pops.text: It started with Sherlock Holmes. Hunter and Garcia were watching the 1959 film of The Hound of the Baskervilles and speculating about the ghostly hound — somebody, possibly Carolyn 'Mountain Girl' Garcia, suggested it might be a dire wolf.
Hunter then dreamt the song. He woke the next morning, grabbed a pencil before he was entirely awake, and wrote the whole lyric down, trying to capture the dream.
Garcia initially set the lyric aside while watching TV, until Hunter protested. Garcia picked up the page and set it to music that same afternoon.
Fast work: the finished song debuted onstage on June 7, 1969 — a full year before it reached an album.
The setting, 'Fennario,' is a place of the imagination borrowed from the folk ballad 'Peggy-O,' descended from the Scottish 'Bonnie Lass o' Fyvie.'

Dark times, dark dedication: at Winterland on October 26, 1969, Garcia dedicated this song to 'the Zodiac cat' — the Zodiac killer, then at large in the Bay Area — 'and also to paranoid fantasies everywhere.'
That crying sound is Garcia on pedal steel. He'd owned one in the Haight and given it up as too hard, then bought a Zane Beck Custom Double-10 in a Denver music store and learned in public.
Singing duties weren't always Garcia's: early on, Bob Weir sometimes sang this one while Garcia played pedal steel instead.
Deadcast guest Gary Lambert calls it 'the peppiest murder ballad ever written' — scary, ominous lyrics delivered with good cheer and wit. Spot the smile, fear the teeth.
It became a first-set staple: 226 performances between 1969 and 1995, played every year except 1975, with acoustic versions getting more common later on.

title: Dire Wolf

description: One of the last Garcia-Hunter songs, debuted live in February 1993 and never finished in the studio before Garcia's death. This official video is RFK Stadium that June, with Bruce Hornsby sitting in on accordion.

pops.text: Late-era Garcia-Hunter: this is one of the final songs the pair added to the Dead's repertoire, arriving in a strong 1992-93 batch alongside 'So Many Roads,' 'Days Between' and 'Liberty.'
Garcia told Guitar Player in 1993 he wasn't sure if it was 'going to be a shuffle or what' — he wrote it trying things out on keyboard, because stylistically it was wide open.
The band workshopped it fast: a Club Front rehearsal was taped on February 18, 1993 — just three days before the live debut. That rehearsal was later released on the So Many Roads box set.
Live debut: February 21, 1993 at the Oakland Coliseum Arena, slotted in the first set between 'Greatest Story Ever Told' and fellow debut 'Eternity.' 'Liberty' debuted at the same show.
It was a two-day songwriting flood: four of the songs on 2019's Ready or Not — this one, 'Liberty,' 'Eternity' and 'Days Between' — debuted across back-to-back February 1993 shows.
Hunter's place names are invented poetry: Sycamore Slough, Shadowfall Ward and Seminole Square appear to be fictitious, per the Annotated Grateful Dead Lyrics.
This video is RFK Stadium, Washington, DC, June 26, 1993. Archivist David Lemieux calls this performance 'a classic of the late-era Garcia-Hunter output.'
Spot the guest: Bruce Hornsby sits in on accordion here — even though he had left the Dead's touring lineup more than a year earlier, he rejoined them for these DC shows.
It was played 65 times in all, and it never really left rotation — right through to the band's final show in Chicago on July 9, 1995.

The studio version that never was: it was earmarked for the Dead's unfinished 14th studio album. In 2019, Ready or Not — curated by Lemieux to imagine that album — finally gave it an album home, using a March 1993 Chapel Hill performance.

title: Lazy River Road

description: R.E.M.'s breakthrough hit from Document (1987): a jangling rocker that sounds like a love dedication but is really about using people. Stipe's one-word 'Fire!' chorus helped take the Athens band into the US Top 10 for the first time.

pops.text: Out before the album: the single landed on August 24, 1987, a week ahead of Document, the band's fifth album, on I.R.S. Records.
A true four-way write: Bill Berry, Peter Buck, Mike Mills and Michael Stipe all share the credit. It was recorded in April 1987 at Sound Emporium in Nashville.
Porch music: Peter Buck came up with the song's opening riff while sitting on his front porch, according to American Songwriter's account of the song.
Not a love song: Stipe told Musician magazine in January 1988 that it was 'incredibly violent' and 'very clear that it's about using people over and over again.'
Spot the swap: the song has just three verses and the first two are identical. In the third, 'A simple prop to occupy my time' becomes 'Another prop has occupied my time.'
The whole chorus is one word — 'Fire' — repeated over Mike Mills singing the backing line 'She's coming down on her own now.'
Document was R.E.M.'s first album co-produced with Scott Litt, the start of a six-album partnership. It peaked at No. 10 on the Billboard 200 and became their first platinum album.
Breakthrough numbers: No. 9 on the Billboard Hot 100 — the band's first hit single — plus No. 2 on Mainstream Rock Tracks and No. 6 in New Zealand. In the UK it stalled at No. 51 first time around.
Artist behind the camera: the video was directed by artist Robert Longo. Its director of photography was Alton Brown, years before he became a Food Network star.
Second chances: a 1991 UK re-release took it to No. 16, and gamers got it too — it appears in Guitar Hero World Tour (2008) and Rock Band 4 (2015).

title: The One I Love

description: A Southern Gothic chamber-pop broadside from The Tortured Poets Department, written alone at the piano about being raised famous and then judged for it. Track 10, solo-written, and produced by Swift with Jack Antonoff.

pops.text: Track 10 on The Tortured Poets Department, Swift's 11th studio album, released April 19, 2024. No music video was made — this official lyric video is the visual.
She wrote it entirely alone, at the piano. In her Amazon Music commentary, Swift said she was in a bitter state, reflecting on how her teenage rise to stardom shaped how she sees herself.
Solo writer, two producers: Swift and Jack Antonoff. Antonoff's credit list is a band in itself — synths, drums, bass, electric guitar, piano and even cello.
Title watch: critics noted the echo of Edward Albee's 1962 play Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? — itself a riff on the Big Bad Wolf song from Disney's Three Little Pigs.
The sound is Southern Gothic chamber pop: dense echo and strings, twangy electric guitars and galloping synths across 5 minutes 34 seconds, with a resonating Moog bass in the bridge.
The imagery flips between witch and circus animal — leaping from the gallows in one line, then 'I was tame, I was gentle, 'til the circus life made me mean' in another.
Her point, in her own commentary: society claims a 'sense of ownership' over public figures — 'We put them through hell… we love to watch artists in pain' — then judges what they create from it.
Rolling Stone's Rob Sheffield called it a 'luridly comic goth-horror melodrama of girlhood in America' — the evil twin of 'Mirrorball,' filtered through Mary Shelley's Frankenstein.
Chart feat: it debuted at No. 9 on the Hot 100 in the week Tortured Poets tracks took the entire top 14 — a first in chart history. It also hit No. 9 on the Global 200.

On the Eras Tour from Paris in May 2024, she sang it atop a moving glass platform fans dubbed the 'TayRoomba.' When it malfunctioned in New Orleans that October, she hopped off and improvised new choreography without missing a beat.

title: Who’s Afraid of Little Old Me?
